newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: "I apologise," ex-Irish PM Haughey tells tribunal.
newsitem.headline: "I apologise," ex-Irish PM Haughey tells tribunal.

text.p: Former Irish Prime Minister Charles Haughey apologised to a tribunal on Tuesday for denying that he received more than a million pounds (dollars) from a department store tycoon.

The 71-year-old Haughey, three times leader of his country, told the tribunal that he was sorry he had told the panel through his lawyers that he had not received any money from Ben Dunne, whose family controls the Dunnes Stores retail chain.

It was Haughey's first appearance at the tribunal, which began its work after media revelations about mysterious payments to politicians which forced Michael Lowry, then transport minister, to resign at the end of last year.
He said "I apologise" after acknowledging that until eight days ago he had instructed his lawyers to deny receiving 1.3 million pounds ($2.0 million) from Dunne between 1989 and 1992.
Haughey's last term as prime minister ran from 1987 to 1992.

Never shy of publicity in a career that made him one of the most powerful politicians in modern Irish history, he arrived two hours early at Dublin Castle, where the tribunal sits, to avoid a posse of photographers.
He told the Justice McCracken, who heads the investigation, that his financial affairs were handled by his late friend and former partner in an accountancy firm, Des Traynor.
Haughey, who now lives in retirement in a private mansion, said that during his time in office he did not keep a close personal eye on his money, which was handled by Traynor.

Because of this, Haughey said, he was unaware of who his benefactors were and had told his lawyers to deny receiving the money until he had been given a full set of documents from the tribunal's work.

Last week his legal team read a statement from Haughey in which he admitted misleading both his lawyers and the tribunal. It was the first time had had admitted receiving cash from Dunne in a scandal that has captivated the public for months.

Haughey said Dunne had not asked for political favours and none had been given. Dunne told the tribunal this year that he had given the money to Haughey because the latter had acute financial problems.
Haughey, in a charcoal-grey suit, appeared a little hard of hearing and asked several times to have questions repeated.
The tribunal was set up last year after media reports that a senior ex-minister of the powerful Fianna Fail party had been given 1.3 million pounds by Dunne.
Lowry, then in the government of former Prime Minister John Bruton, resigned shortly after admitting that Dunne paid for the renovation and extension of his private home.
Bruton authorised the establishment of the tribunal, which has heard evidence from all major political parties of huge donations by Dunne for campaign expenses and election funding.
It led to calls for an investigation into the financing of political parties, and for a register to be kept on links between business and politicians.
There has been no suggestion by Dunne or the tribunal that political favours were asked for or bought, and Dunne told the panel that he was merely using a personal fortune to help those concerned.
The Dunnes Stores chain owns green-fronted department stores in every town and city of Ireland and is controlled by family members who dropped Ben Dunne from the business five years ago.
